Borrowed from French sous-verre.
Borrowed from French souvenir.

parole.significato: success (the fact of getting or achieving respect or fame)
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from French succès.
From French surréalisme (“surrealism”).
Borrowed from French soutien.

parole.significato: attic (space, often unfinished and with sloped walls, directly below the roof)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French soffite (“soffit”), from Italian soffitto, from Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”).
Borrowed from French soupe.

parole.significato: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see σπάω (spáo), τον (ton), πάγο (págo).
parole.testo: Calque of French briser la glace.
Transliteration of French sport, itself borrowed from English sport.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek σταδιοδρομία (stadiodromía, “stadium race”) with semantic loan from French carrière.

parole.significato: stabilizer (any substance added to something in order to stabilize it)
parole.testo: Learnedly from σταθεροποιώ (statheropoió) + -τής (-tís), a calque of French stabilisateur.
Learnedly, from Hellenistic Koine Greek σταθμεύω (stathmeúō, “take up quarters”), from σταθμός (stathmós) + -εύω (-eúō), with semantic loan from French stationner.
Calque of French stéatopygie. From Ancient Greek στέαρ (stéar, “hard fat, suet”) + the interfix -ο- (-o-) + πῡγ(ή) (pūg(ḗ), “buttocks”) + the suffix -ία (-ía). First attested in 1896.
Borrowed from French stéréotype.
Learned borrowing from French stéthoscope, from Ancient Greek στῆθος (stêthos, “breast”) + σκοπέω (skopéō, “look at”).

parole.significato: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see στην (stin), άκρη (ákri), της (tis), γλώσσας (glóssas).
parole.termine_origine: sur le bout de la langue

catena.termine: sur le bout de la langue

parole.testo: Calque of French sur le bout de la langue.
Semantic loan from French couche. As in accusative στῐβάδα (stĭbáda) of Ancient Greek στῐβάς (“bed of straw”). The stem στι- by dissimilation from στείβω (steíbō, “I tread”).
From the French stœchiologie.
Learnedly from στόχ(ος) (stóch(os)) + -εύω (-évo), a calque of French viser.

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατηγική (stratēgikḗ), the feminine nominative singular of στρατηγικός (stratēgikós, “of a general”), with semantic loan from French stratégie for non-military contexts.

parole.significato: military (describing members of the armed forces)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek στρατιωτικός (stratiōtikós), from στρατιώτης (stratiṓtēs) + -ικός (-ikós), with semantic loan from French militaire.
στρεπτός (streptós, “rotatable, twisted”) + κόκκος (kókkos, “particle”), calque of French streptocoque, itself from the equivalent Ancient Greek words.
From French stylographe (“pen”).
Borrowed from French stylo (“pen”), which is an abbreviation of stylographe (“pen”), from English stylograph.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συγγνώμη (sungnṓmē) and semantic loan from French pardon.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συγκεκριμένος (sunkekriménos), perfect passive participle of Ancient Greek συγκρίνω (sunkrínō). With semantic loan from French concret.
συν- (syn-) + κέντρο (kéntro) + -ώνω (-óno), formed as a calque of French concentrer. First attested in 1814.

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συγκλίνω (sunklínō, “to reconcile”), from Ancient Greek συγκλίνω (sunklínō, “to lay together”), with semantic loan from French converger. By surface analysis, συγ- (syg-) + κλίνω (klíno).
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συγχρονισμός (sunkhronismós, “agreement of time”) < Ancient Greek συγχρονίζω (sunkhronízō) and semantic loan from French synchronisation and simultanéité.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συγχωνεύω (sunkhōneúō, “to melt down”) with semantic loan from French fusionner. By surface analysis, συγ- (syg-) + χωνεύω (chonévo).

From συζυτ(ώ) (syzyt(ó)) + modern suffix -άω (-áo). Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συζητῶ (suzētô), contracted form of συζητέω (suzētéō, “examine together with”), from συ- (su-) + ζητέω (zētéō). Also, a semantic loan from French discuter.
Learnedly from σύζυγ(ος) (sýzyg(os)) + -ικός (-ikós), a calque of French conjugal.
From Ancient Greek συλλέγω. Sense make a collection, semantic loan from French collectionner.

From Hellenistic Koine Greek συλλέκτης, from συλλέγω (sullégō, “collect”). Morphologically, from συλ- (συν-) (“plus”) + λέγω (“ancient sense: choose”) Sense collector of items, semantic loan from French collectionneur. Sense apparatus for collection, semantic loan from French collecteur.

parole.significato: compromise (the settlement of differences by arbitration or by consent reached by mutual concessions)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμβιβασμός (sumbibasmós, “conciliation, reconciliation”) with semantic loan from French compromis and English compromise. By surface analysis, συμβιβασ- (stem of συμβιβάζω (symvivázo)) + -μός (-mós).
Learned borrowing from French symbiotique. By surface analysis, συμβιωτ(ής) (symviot(ís)) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συμβολή (sumbolḗ) with semantic loan from French contribution.

parole.significato: to symbolize (to be symbolic of; to represent)
parole.testo: Learnedly from σύμβολ(ο) (sýmvol(o)) + -ίζω (-ízo), a calque of French symboliser.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμβολικός (sumbolikós) with semantic loan from French symbolique. By surface analysis, σύμβολο (sýmvolo) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: symbolism (representation of a concept through symbols or underlying meanings of objects or qualities)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French symbolisme. By surface analysis, σύμβολ(ο) (sýmvol(o)) + -ισμός (-ismós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συμβουλευτικός (sumbouleutikós) with semantic loan from French consultatif. By surface analysis, συμβουλεύ(ω) (symvoulév(o)) + -τικός (-tikós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σῠμβουλεύομαι (sŭmbouleúomai) with semantic loan from French consulter.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμμετοχή (summetokhḗ, “share”) with semantic loan from French participation.

Learned borrowing from French symétrique, from symétr(ie) < Ancient Greek συμμετρ(ία) f (summetr(ía)) + -ique < -ικός (-ikós) A different sense for the Hellenistic συμμετρικός (summetrikós, “of moderate size”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συμμορία (summoría, “symmoria”), with semantic loan from French bande in the sense 'gang, band'.

parole.significato: to conform, to make conform, to make comply
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμμορφῶ (summorphô, “give the same form”) with -ώνω (-óno) ending and semantic loan from French se conformer.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμμόρφωσις (summórphōsis) with semantic loan from French conformité and English conformity. By surface analysis, συμμορφώνω (symmorfóno) + -ση (-si).

parole.significato: compression (the act of compressing, or the state of being compressed)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συμπίεσις (sumpíesis) with -ση (-si) ending and semantic loan from French compression. By surface analysis, συμπιέζω (sympiézo) + -ση (-si).

parole.significato: complementary (acting as a complement; making up a whole with something else)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συμπληρωματικός (sumplērōmatikós) with semantic loan from French complémentaire and supplémentaire. By surface analysis, συμπληρωματ- (stem of συμπλήρωμα (symplíroma)) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from French symptomatique. By surface analysis, from the συμπτωματ- stem of σύμπτωμα (sýmptoma) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συμφοιτητής (sumphoitētḗs) with semantic loan from French condisciple. By surface analysis, συμ- (sym-) + φοιτητής (foititís).

parole.significato: the result of mixing up of dissimilar elements
parole.testo: From Hellenistic Koine Greek συμφῡρμός (sumphūrmós) from verb συμφύρω (sumphúrō). For sense in linguistics, calque of French contamination.

Learned borrowing from Byzantine Greek συνάδελφος (sunádelphos, “member of a (military) company”), from Ancient Greek συνάδελφος (sunádelphos, “who has siblings”), with semantic loan from French confrère. By surface analysis, συν- (syn-) + αδελφός (adelfós).

parole.significato: consistency (reliability or uniformity; the quality of being consistent)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συνέπεια (sunépeia, “connection of words”), from συν- (sun-) + ἔπ(ος) (ép(os)) + -εια (-eia), with semantic loan from French suite and conséquence.
From Ancient Greek συνέρχομαι (“come together, assemble, meet”). Morphologically, from συν- (“together”) + έρχομαι (“come”). For sense: recover: Semantic loan from French revenir à soi

parole.significato: alert (state of readiness in case of emergency)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συναγερμός (sunagermós, “concentration”), with semantic loan from French alarme.
Learnedly from the συναισθηματ- stem of συναίσθημα (synaísthima, “emotion, sentiment”) + -ικός (-ikós), with semantic loan from French sentimental.
Reborrowing from French syndicat, itself formed from Ancient Greek σύνδικος (súndikos, “advocate, barrister”) + a Latinate suffix -at.
From Ancient Greek συνδρομή (sundromḗ). For the modern sense of "help", semantic loan from French secours.

parole.significato: session, sitting, meeting (of a committee, council, etc. to conduct business)
parole.testo: Learnedly from συνεδριάζω (synedriázo) + -ση (-si), a calque of French séance and German Sitzung.

parole.significato: conscious (deliberate, intentional, done with awareness of what one is doing)
parole.testo: Learnedly from συνείδη(ση) (syneídi(si)) + -τός (-tós), a calque of French conscient.
First attested around 1871. From συνέπεια (synépeia) + -ής (-ís), calque of French conséquent.

parole.significato: continuous, contiguous, abutting, adjacent (without intervening space)
parole.testo: Learnedly formed as a passive present participle of Ancient Greek συνέχω (sunékhō, “to hold/keep together”). A calque of French contigu.

parole.significato: to accompany, go with, escort, chaperone
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek συνοδεύω (sunodeúō, “to travel in company”) with semantic loan from French accompagner.

parole.significato: total (entire; relating to the whole of something)
parole.testo: Learnedly from σύνολ(ο) (sýnol(o)) + -ικός (-ikós), a calque of French entier and en totalité.

parole.significato: to converse, to have a discussion
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek συνομιλῶ (sunomilô), contracted form of συνομιλέω (sunomiléō), with semantic loan from French converser.
Borrowed from French sphygmographie. By surface analysis, σφυγμός (sfygmós, “pulse”) + -γραφία (-grafía, “-graphy”).

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σχέσις (skhésis), from the aorist stem σχε- (skhe-) of ἔχω (ékhō, “to have, hold”) + -σις (-sis). The modern sense of "relation" is a semantic loan from French relation.

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σχίσμα (skhísma) (Hellenisitic sense "division of ecclesiastical unity"), from verb σχίζω (skhízō), stem σχισ- + -μα (-ma). For sense "division of a group of political party" a semantic loan from French schisme.

Semantic loan from French esquisser or dessiner, or English design. Learnedly, from Ancient Greek σχεδιάζω (skhediázō, “do a thing offhand”), from σχέδιον (skhédion), neuter of σχέδιος (skhédios, “casual, offhand”). : figurative sense "plan": Semantic loan from English plan

parole.significato: to relate, to associate (to bring into a relation, association, or connection)
parole.testo: Learnedly from σχετικός (schetikós) + -ίζω (-ízo), with semantic loan from French mettre en relation (active) and être en relations (passive).

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek σχετικός (skhetikós); synchronically analyzable as an adjectival derivative of σχέση (schési, “relation”). Τhe modern sense of "relative, proportional" is a semantic loan from French relatif.

parole.significato: to form, make, create, organize, shape
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σχηματίζω (skhēmatízō). Partially possibly a semantic loan from French former.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek or Byzantine Greek σχολιάζω (skholiázō) with semantic loan from French commenter. By surface analysis, σχόλι(ο) (schóli(o)) + -άζω (-ázo).

parole.significato: somatology (the study of the physical nature of human beings)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French somatologie or English somatology. By surface analysis, σώμα (sóma) + -λογία (-logía).

parole.significato: convocation; the act of convoking; convening, assembling; gathering a congregation; summoning others, calling together…
parole.testo: Calque of French convocation from Latin convocātiō, con- (“with, together”) + vocātiō (“calling, summons”), hence literally συγ- (syg-, “with, together”) + κλήση (klísi, “calling, summons”); from Byzantine Greek σύγκλησις (súnklēsis) from roots of the verb συγκαλώ (sygkaló) from Koine Greek σῠγκᾰλῶ

parole.significato: agreement, contract (legally binding pact between two or more parties)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμβασις (súmbasis) with -ση (-si) ending and semantic loan from French convention.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμβολον (súmbolon) with semantic loan from French symbole.

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύνθημα (súnthēma) with semantic loan from French signal and Italian segnale in the sense 'signal', from French mot d'ordre in the sense 'watchword, motto' and from English slogan.
Inherited from Ancient Greek σύντροφος (súntrophos), from συν- (sun-) + τρέφω (tréphō) + -ος (-os), with semantic loan from French compagnon and Italian compagno.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σῦριγξ (sûrinx, “pan pipes”). The medical term is a reborrowing/semantic loan from French seringue (“syringe”)

parole.significato: twitch, spasm, contraction, convulsion (involuntary muscular movement)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύσπασις (súspasis) with -ση (-si) suffix and semantic loan from French contraction.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τά(σις) (tá(sis), “stretching, tension”) + -ση (-si). The sense ‘voltage, potential difference’ is a semantic loan from French tension. See τείνω (teíno).
Borrowed from French thé. Doublet of τσάι (tsái).

parole.significato: skirt suit (consisting of a suit coat, η ζακέτα (zakéta), and skirt, η φούστα (foústa))
parole.testo: From French tailleur (“woman's suit”).
Borrowed from French tact.

parole.significato: to organise, arrange, settle, sort out, fix (to put into an orderly sequence or arrangement or to plan)
parole.testo: From τακτ(ός) (takt(ós), “arranged, fixed, set”) + -ο- + -ποιώ (-poió, “to make”). First part from the ancient τάξη (táxē, “order”)/τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange, to put in order”) and suffix from the ancient ποιέω (poiéō) / ποιῶ. First attested in 1855, a calque of French mettre en ordre.

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ταμεῖον (tameîon), from Ancient Greek ταμιεῖον (tamieîon, “treasury, storehouse, closet”), with semantic loan from French caisse and semantic loan from Latin thesaurus.
Borrowed from French tableau (“board”).
Borrowed from French taxi.
Learnedly from the ταξινομη- stem of ταξινομώ (taxinomó) + -ση (-si), a calque of French taxinomie.
Borrowed from French tarot.
Borrowed from French tatouage.
The general sense is from Ancient Greek ταὐτότης (tautótēs), equivalent to ταὐτό (taftó, “the self”) + -ότητα (-ótita, “-ity, -ness”). The mathematics sense is a calque of French identité.
From ταχυ- (tachy-, “fast”) + δάκτυλο (dáktylo, “finger”) + -ία (-ía), calque of French prestidigitation. First attested 1872.
From ταχυ- (tachy-, “fast”) + δάκτυλο (dáktylo, “finger”) + -ουργός (-ourgós, “worker”), calque of French prestidigitateur. First attested 1874.
Borrowed from French téléphérique.

parole.significato: tense (characterized by strain (on the nerves, emotions, etc.))
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τεταμένος (tetaménos, “stretched, pulled taut”), passive perfect participle of τείνω (teíno), with semantic loan from French tendu.
Calque of French technologie, from Ancient Greek τέχνη (tékhnē) + -λογία (-logía).
Calque of French technologue from technologie. The Hellenistic Koine τεχνολόγος has different sense: ("treating art rules, or rhetoric writer").
Calque of French téléspectateur, from Ancient Greek τῆλε (têle, “far off, tele-”) + θεατής (theatís, “spectator”).
From τηλ(ε)- (til(e)-, “far, tele-”) + εργασία (ergasía, “job, profession, work”), calque of French télétravail or calque of English teleworking.

parole.significato: telescopic (pertaining to, or carried out by means of, a telescope)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French télescopique or English telescopic. By surface analysis, τηλεσκόπιο (tileskópio) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from French téléphonique or English telephonic. By surface analysis, τηλέφων(ο) (tiléfon(o)) + -ικός (-ikós).
Borrowed from French téléphoner or English telephone; by surface analysis, τηλέφωνο (tiléfono) + -ώ (-ó).

parole.significato: television (the display device, the shows displayed and the industry in which shows are made)
parole.testo: From τηλε- (tile-, “far, tele-”) + όραση (órasi, “vision”), a calque of French télévision.

parole.significato: to abide (by), to adhere (to), to comply (with), to keep (to), to observe, to respect, to stick (to) (to follow or obey…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τηρῶ (tērô), with semantic loan from French garder (“keep”).
Learned borrowing from French turquoise (“turquoise -gemstone-”).
Borrowed from French tire-bouchon.
Learnedly from the Katharevousa dative plural form ταις προάλλαις (tais proállais), itself a calque of French ces derniers jours.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τομεύς (tomeús, “one that cuts”) + accusative case ending -έα (-éa), from τέμνω (témnō, “to cut”), with semantic loan from French secteur.

parole.significato: to accent, to accentuate (to mark with a written stress mark)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek τονίζω (tonízō) with semantic loan from French accentuer. By surface analysis, τόνος (tónos) + -ίζω (-ízo).

Learned borrowing from Byzantine Greek τοπίον (topíon), from Koine Greek τόπιον (tópion) with shift of accent to -ίον (-íon), with semantic loan from French paysage or Semantic loan from Italian paesaggio.

parole.significato: local (from or in a nearby location)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek τοπῐκός (topĭkós) with semantic loan from French topique (in the medical sense) and local.
From French torpille. First attested 1879.

parole.significato: toilet, lavatory, WC (the fixture and the room)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French toilette.
Borrowed from French toucan, borrowed from Old Tupi tukana, from Proto-Tupi-Guarani *tũkãn, from Proto-Tupian *jɨokãn.
Participle of τρέχω (trécho). Learnedly, from Ancient Greek τρέχων (trékhōn) & semantic loan from French courant. Also substantivised by ellipsis of a noun.
Borrowed from French tricot (“knitting”).

Learned borrowing from French tricycle from Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-) & κύκλος (kúklos). By surface analysis, τρί- (trí-) + κύκλ(ος) (kýkl(os)) + suffix -ο for neuters. Also see the adjective τρίκυκλος (tríkyklos).
Borrowed from French travesti.

parole.significato: to cause someone to have stage fright
parole.testo: Borrowed from French traquer in the sense: I have trac / traque.
Borrowed from French tracteur.
From Byzantine Greek τρελός (trelós), from Koine Greek τρηρός (trērós), from Ancient Greek τρήρων (trḗrōn). The chess sense is a semantic loan from French fou.

parole.significato: terrorist (person, group, or organization that uses violent action, or the threat of violent action, to further politic…
parole.testo: τρόμος (trómos, “terror, fear”) + -κράτης (-krátis, “-crat, -ist”), calque of French terroriste. First attested 1850.

parole.significato: terrorism, terror (commission of an act of violence to create a political or emotional response)
parole.testo: τρόμος (trómos, “terror, fear”) + -κρατία (-kratía, “-cracy, -ism”), calque of French terrorisme. First attested 1840.
From French trotteuse. Compare with English streetwalker, Serbo-Croatian uličarka.

parole.significato: Trotskyism (political doctrine/philosophy named after Leon Trosky)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French trotskisme.
Learnedly, from the Hellenistic Koine Greek τροχιά (trokhiá, “wheel-track; path”), from the ancient τροχ(ός) (trokh(ós), “wheel”) + -ιά (-iá). For sense orbit, semantic loan from French orbite.
Borrowed from French tonne (“ton”).

parole.significato: sort, type, mould, stamp (of a person character)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos). The colloquial meaning of "guy, chap" is a semantic loan from French type. Sense "the press", semantic loan from French presse.

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑγροποιῶ (hugropoiô), contracted form of ὑγροποιέω (hugropoiéō, “to moisten”), with semantic loan from French liquéfier. By surface analysis, υγρός (ygrós) + -ποιώ (-poió).
Learnedly from υδατ(ο)- (ydat(o)-) + άνθρακας (ánthrakas), a calque of French hydrates de carbone.
Learnedly from υδρογόν(ο) (ydrogón(o), “hydrogen”) + άνθρακας (ánthrakas, “carbon”), a calque of French hydrocarbure.
From French hydrogène, a French-coined term adopted into Greek, equivalent to υδρο- (ydro-, “water, hydro-”) + γόνος (gónos, “progeny, offspring”). First attested 1871.
Learned borrowing from French hydroélectrique. By surface analysis, υδρο- (ydro-) + ηλεκτρικός (ilektrikós).
From υδρο- (ydro-, “water related”) + πέπων (pépon, “melon”), a calque of French melon d'eau.
Learnedly from υδρό- (ydró-) + -γειος (-geios), a calque of French terraqué.
Borrowed from French hydrophile, a French-coined term adopted into Greek, equivalent to υδρό- (ydró-, “water, hydro-”) + -φιλος (-filos, “friend of, -phile”). First attested 1888.

Learnedly, from Hellenistic Koine Greek υἱοθετέω (huiothetéō) / υἱοθετῶ (huiothetô). The figurative sense, semantic loan from French adopter. Morphologically, from υιός (yiós, “son”) (υἱός (huiós)) + θέτω (théto, “put, place”) (from τίθημι (títhēmi)).
ύλη (ýli, “material”) + -ιστής (-istís, “-ist, -er”), calque of French matérialiste. First attested 1794.
From French hylozoïsme.
From the French hylozoïsme. With internal borrowing of original Greek combining forms: ὕλη (“matter”) for hylo- + ζωή (“life”) + Hellenistic -ισμός for -isme.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπάλληλος (hupállēlos, “subordinate”). The "employee" sense is a semantic loan from French employé.
From Ancient Greek ὑπέρτασις (hupértasis). By surface analysis, υπέρ (ypér) + τάση (tási). Semantic loan from French hypertension.

parole.significato: forming nouns and adjectives denoting the maximum proportion of oxygen or highest oxidation state of the central atom i…
parole.testo: From French per- in the chemical sense, under the paretymological influence of ὑπερ- (huper-).

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑπεράνθρωπος (huperánthrōpos, “superior to man”) with semantic loan from French surhumain and German Übermensch. By surface analysis, υπερ- (yper-) + άνθρωπος (ánthropos).
From υπερ- (yper-, “ultra”) + ιώδης (iódis, “violet”), calque of French ultraviolet.
From υπερ- (yper-) + μαγγάνιο (mangánio) + -ικός (-ikós), calque of French permanganate where the prefix per- has been paretymologically attributed as υπερ- (yper-).

parole.significato: surrealism (the artistic movement and aesthetic philosophy)
parole.testo: From υπερ- (yper-, “super-, ultra-, sur-”) + ρεαλισμός (realismós, “realism”), calque of French surréalisme.

parole.significato: hypertrophy (increase in the size of an organ due to swelling of the individual cells)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French hypertrophie, a French-coined term adopted into Greek, equivalent to υπερ- (yper-, “over, hyper-”) + τροφ(ή) (trof(í), “food, nourishment”) + -ία (-ía). First attested 1856.
From υπερώα (yperóa) + -ικός (-ikós). Calque of French vélaire.
From Ancient Greek ὑπερωκεάνιος (huperōkeánios); by surface analysis, υπερ- (yper-) + ωκεάνιο (okeánio). The modern sense of "ocean liner" is a semantic loan from French transocéanien.

Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑπηρετῶ (hupēretô), contracted form of ὑπηρετέω (hupēretéō, “to do (rower's) service”), with semantic loan from French servir. By surface analysis, υπηρέτης (ypirétis) + -ω (-o).
Calque of French somnambule. From ύπν(ος) (“sleeping”) + -ο- + -βάτης (“walker”).
Learnedly from υπνώ(νω) (ypnó(no)) + -τήριο (-tírio), a calque of French dortoir.

parole.significato: to submit, to put (to present for approval, consideration, assessment, etc.)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑποβάλλω (hupobállō) with semantic loan from French soumettre and suggérer.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ῠ̔πογρᾰ́φω (hŭpogrắphō) and semantic loan from French souscrire and signer. By surface analysis, υπο- (ypo-, “under”) + γράφω (gráfo, “write”).

parole.significato: to foment, to stir up (to incite)
parole.testo: Learnedly from υπο- (ypo-) + δαυλ(ός) (davl(ós)) + -ίζω (-ízo), a calque of French attiser.
From Ancient Greek ὑποδομή (hupodomḗ). Semantic loan from French infrastructure.
υποκειμενικός (ypokeimenikós, “subjective”) + -ότητα (-ótita, “-ity, -ness”), calque of French subjectivité.

From Ancient Greek ὑπολογίζομαι (“take under consideration”). By surface analysis, υπο- (ypo-, “hypo-, under”) + λογίζομαι (logízomai, “count, reckon, consider”). Also, semantic loan from French calculer.
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑπολογισμός (hupologismós, “taking into account”) with semantic loan from French calcul. By surface analysis, υπολογίζω (ypologízo) + -μός (-mós).

parole.significato: self-seeker, selfish person (person who calculates before acting)
parole.testo: Calque of French calculateur (“calculating person”), after English electronic calculator, using υπολογίζω (ypologízo, “to calculate”) + -τής (-tís).

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑποστηρίζω (hupostērízō), with semantic loan from French soutenir, appuyer, as well as semantic loan from English support. By surface analysis, υπο- (ypo-) + στηρίζω (stirízo).
Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑποτάσσω (hupotássō) with semantic loan from French subordonner.

parole.significato: devaluation, depreciation (the removal or lessening of something's value)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑποτίμησις (hupotímēsis) with semantic loan from French dépréciation, dévaluation. By surface analysis, υποτίμη- (ypotími-, stem of υποτιμώ (ypotimó)) + -ση (-si).

parole.significato: to depreciate, to bring down, to mark down (prices)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑποτιμῶ (hupotimô), contracted form of ὑποτιμάω (hupotimáō), with semantic loan from French déprécier and dévaluer.

Verb formed from the adjective υπόχρεος (ypóchreos) (from Ancient Greek ὑπόχρεος (hupókhreos, “indebted”), from υπο- (upo-) + χρέος (khréos)), + -ώνω (suffix for verbs). For sense "oblige", calque of French obliger.

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ὑποχωρητικός (hupokhōrētikós, “modest, self-effacing”) with semantic adaptation to the modern meanings of υποχωρώ (ypochoró) and semantic loan from French régressif in the phonetic sense. By surface analysis, υποχωρη- (stem of υποχωρώ (ypochoró)) + -τικός (-tikós).

parole.significato: subtitle (a heading below or after a title)
parole.testo: Learnedly from υπο- (ypo-) + τίτλος (títlos), a calque of French sous-titre.

parole.significato: deputy minister, undersecretary, state secretary (minister ranking below the minister in charge of a department or mini…
parole.testo: Learnedly from υφ- (yf-) + υπουργός (ypourgós), a calque of French sous-ministre.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὑψίπεδον (hupsípedon), neuter of ὑψίπεδος (hupsípedos, adjective), with semantic loan from French haut plateau and German Hochebene.
From French favori.

parole.significato: sideburns (in plural, chiefly US), sideboards (in plural, UK), sidelevers (in plural, Australia)
parole.testo: From French favorites.
Borrowed from French fanatique.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φαρμακευτικός (pharmakeutikós) with semantic loan from French pharmaceutique.

Calque of French pharmacologie from φάρμακο (fármako) + -λογία (-logía) from Ancient Greek φάρμᾰκον (phármăkon, “potion, drug, medicine”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, abstract noun suffix).
From φατνίο (fatnío, “tooth socket”) + -ακός (-akós). Calque of French alvéolaire.
From French féminisme, from Latin femina (“woman”).
From French féministe.
Borrowed from French fennec, from Arabic فَنَك (fanak), from Classical Persian فنک (fanak), ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *hünegen (“fox”).
Borrowed from French festival.

parole.significato: fetish (something which is believed to possess, contain, or cause spiritual or magical powers)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French fétiche (“fetish”).

Learned borrowing from French phthore (an obsolete early synonym of fluor) derived from Ancient Greek φθορά (phthorá, “deterioration”) on account of the corrosive nature of hydrofluoric acid. Russian фтор (ftor) is also from the same root, in contrast to most European languages which use derivatives

parole.significato: philhellene, Hellenophile (a lover of Greece or Greek culture)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φιλέλλην (philéllēn), from φίλος (phílos) + Έλλην (Éllēn), with semantic loan from French philhellènes, from the plural of the same etymon, in the sense 'supporter of Greek independence'.

parole.significato: philanthropic, charitable (relating to charitable organisations or people)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French philanthropique, from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, φιλάνθρωπος (filánthropos) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: philhellenic, philhellene, Hellenophile (loving Greece or Greek culture)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French philhellénique. By surface analysis, φιλέλλην(ας) (filéllin(as)) + -ικός (-ikós).
Learned borrowing from French philologique. By surface analysis, φιλολογ(ία) (filolog(ía)) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: to accommodate, to put up, to host
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek φιλοξενῶ (philoxenô), contracted form of φιλοξενέω (philoxenéō), with semantic loan from French hospitaliser (in its rare and dated meaning 'to give hospitality') and English host.
Learned borrowing from French philatéliste. By surface analysis, φιλοτελ(ισμός) (filotel(ismós)) + -ιστής (-istís).
Borrowed from French fixer + -άρω (“suffix for verbs”).
Calque of French flûte à bec.
From French flipper, from English flip.
Learned borrowing from French flou.
Borrowed from French fond de teint.
From French fondamentaliste.
Borrowed from French framboise.

parole.significato: prepared by shaking to produce cold drink with foam
parole.testo: Borrowed from French frappé.

parole.significato: to riffle, leaf through, flip through (the pages of a book)
parole.testo: φύλλο (fýllo, “leaf, page”) + μετρώ/μετράω (metró/metráo, “measure”), a free translation of French feuilleter.
Learned translation of French photographie. Morphologically, from φωτο- (“photo”) + -γραφ- (“-graphy”) + -ία; see φως (fos, “light”), γραφή (grafí, “writing”) for more.
From φωτογραφ(ία) (“photograph”) + -ίζω. Also + -ώ for the more formal variation φωτογραφώ. Calque of French photographier.
First attested around 1848. Calque of French phototypie: φωτο- (foto-) + -τυπία (-typía).
A reborrowing from French phonème (“phoneme”), from Ancient Greek φώνημα (phṓnēma, “sound made, utterance; thing spoken, speech, language”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos). For sense disorder, mess, semantic loan from French chaos (in that sense) from Latin chaos, from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).

Learned borrowing from French gamin. First attested in the 1862 Greek translation by Ioannis-Isidoridis Skylitsis of Les Miserables (by Victor Hugo). Apparently, a translation‑neologism, [g] > [x] instead of [γ], trying to avoid the derogatory *γαμίνι, or intended to remind of χαμένο (“lost”).

From Ancient Greek χαράσσω (kharássō) from past tense:‑αξα to present:‑άζω, in the pattern of στάζω (stázō), ἔσταξα (éstaxa, “I dripped”). * Sense make rules, semantic loan from French tracer * Sense dawn break, from mediaeval χαράζει (kharázei)

parole.significato: cartomancy (the supposed prediction of the future with playing cards)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French cartomancie, from carto- + μαντεία f (manteía, “divination”). By surface analysis, χαρτο- (charto-, “card”) + -μαντεία (-manteía, “-mancy”), from χαρτί n (chartí, “paper”) and μαντεία f (manteía, “divination”).
From χαρτο- (charto-, “paper”) + νόμισμα (nómisma, “currency”), a calque of French papier-monnaie or English paper money.
From Koine Greek χαρτοφύλαξ (khartophúlax), from χάρτης (khártēs, “piece of paper”) + φύλαξ (phúlax, “guard”) and semantic loan from French portefeuille or Italian portafoglio.
From χείλος (cheílos) + υπερωικός (yperoïkós). Calque of French labiovélaire or English labiovelar.
χειροκροτώ (cheirokrotó, “to applaud”) + -μα (-ma). Calque of French battement de mains or calque of French applaudissement. Attested since 1835 in plural as χειροκροτήματα (cheirokrotímata).
From χειρ (cheir, “hand”) + -ό- (-ó-) + φρένο (fréno, “brake”)., calque of French frein à main or German Handbremse.
Learned borrowing from French chlorophylle, from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós) + φύλλον (phúllon).
Learned borrowing from French chlore, derived from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”).
Calque of French choline or calque of English choline. Attested since 1854.

parole.significato: to use, employ, put to use, utilise
parole.testo: From χρήσιμ(ος) (chrísim(os), “useful”) + -ο- + -ποιώ (-poió, “make”) from the ancient ποιέω (poiéō)/ποιῶ. Calque of French utiliser.

parole.significato: hue, tone (the shade or quality of a colour)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek χροιά (khroiá) with semantic loan from French ton in the senses not literally connected with colour.
Learned borrowing from French chronomètre, from Ancient Greek χρόνος (khrónos, “time”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”). By surface analysis, χρονό- (chronó-) + μέτρο (métro).
ψευδο- (psevdo-, “pseudo-”) + πάτωμα (pátoma, “floor”), a calque of French faux plancher.
From ψευδ- (psevd-, “pseudo-”) + οροφή (orofí, “ceiling”), a calque of French faux plafond.
Learned borrowing from French pseudonyme, from Ancient Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudṓnumos). Morphologically, ψευδ- (psevd-, “pseudo-”) + -ώνυμο (-ónymo, “name”).

parole.significato: voting form, ballot paper on which a vote is cast
parole.testo: From ψήφ(ος) (psíf(os), “vote, ballot”) + -ο- + δελτίο (deltío, “ticket, coupon”), a calque of French bulletin de vote. First attested 1838 in Katharevousa as ψηφοδέλτιον.

Learned borrowing from French psychiatre, from Ancient Greek ψυχ- (psukh-), ψυχή f (psukhḗ, “soul”) + ἰατρός (iatrós, “physician”). By surface analysis, ψυχ- (psych-, “psych-”) + ιατρός (iatrós, “physician”).
Learned borrowing from French psychasthénie. By surface analysis, ψυχ- (psych-) + ασθένεια (asthéneia).
Learnedly from ψυχ(ασθένεια) (psych(asthéneia)) + ασθενής (asthenís), a calque of French psychasthénique (“psychasthenic”).

Substantivized feminine of ψυχιατρικός (psychiatrikós) < ψυχ- (psych-, “psych-”) + ιατρικός (iatrikós, “medical”). Learned borrowing from French psychiatrie, from psychiatre. See Ancient Greek ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul”) + ἰατρεία (iatreía, “healing”), from ἰάομαι (iáomai, “to heal”).
ψυχ- (psych-, “psyh-”) + ιατρικός (iatrikós, “medical”). A learned borrowing from French psychiatrique, from psychiatrie + -ique. See Ancient Greek ψυχή f (psukhḗ, “soul”) and ἰατρικός (iatrikós).
Learned borrowing from French psychothérapie or German Psychotherapie first attested in 1893. Morphologically, ψυχο- (psycho-, “psyxho- (soul)”) + θεραπεία (therapeía, “treatment”). F
Learned borrowing from French psychologie. Μorphologically ψυχο- (psycho-, “ψυχή soul”) + -λογία (-logía, “-logy”). First attested 1805.
Learned borrowing from French psychologique, from psycholog(ie) + -ique, i.e. ψυχολογ(ία) f (psycholog(ía), “psychology”) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: psychologist (expert in the field of psychology)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from French psychologue. Μorphologically, ψυχο- (psycho-, “ψυχή soul”) + -λόγος (-lógos, “λόγος speech”). First attested 1851.
Α learned borrowing from French sang-froid. Morphologically, ψυχρ- (psychr-, “psychro-, ψυχρός cold”) + αίμ(α) (aím(a), “blood”) + -ία (-ía).

Learned borrowing from French psychose from Ancient Greek ψυχή f (psukhḗ, “soul”), ψυχ- of ψυχο- (psukho-) + -ose after névrose. Different sense for the Hellenistic ψύχωσις f (psúkhōsis, “giving life, animating”).
Inherited from Koine Greek ὡριμάζω (hōrimázō). For the figurative sense, semantic loan from French mûrir.
Learned borrowing from French otorhinolaryngologiste.
From Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós) & semantic loan from French pâle.

parole.significato: ripe, mature, mellow (ready for reaping or gathering, or having attained perfection)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek ὥριμος (hṓrimos, “seasonal, timely”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “season, time”). Some senses a semantic loan from French mûr.
